title: Chapter 50 — Ahab’s Boat and Crew. Fedallah
paragraphs: "Who would have thought it, Flask!" cried Stubb. "If I had only one leg, you wouldn't catch me in a boat — unless maybe to plug the drain-hole with my wooden toe. Oh! He's a wonderful old man!"

"I don't think it so strange, on that account," said Flask. "If his leg were off at the hip, now, that would be a different thing. That would disable him. But he has one knee, and a good part of the other left, you know."
"I don't know about that, little man. I've never yet seen him kneel."

Whale-wise people have often debated whether a whaling captain, given how vital his life is to the success of the voyage, has any right to risk that life in the dangers of the chase itself. In just the same way, Tamerlane's soldiers often argued, with tears in their eyes, whether that priceless life of his should be carried into the thick of the fighting.

But with Ahab the question took on a different angle. Considering that even with two legs a man is but a hobbling creature in times of danger — considering that the pursuit of whales is always conducted under great and extraordinary difficulties, and that every individual moment involves peril — under these circumstances, is it wise for any maimed man to enter a whale-boat in the hunt? As a general rule, the joint-owners of the Pequod must plainly have thought not.

Ahab knew well that although his friends at home would think little of his getting into a boat during certain comparatively harmless turns of the chase, for the sake of being near the action and giving his orders in person, yet for Captain Ahab to have a boat actually assigned to him as a regular headsman in the hunt — above all, for Captain Ahab to be supplied with five extra men as that boat's crew — he knew well that such generous notions never entered the heads of the owners of the Pequod. So he had not asked them for a boat's crew, nor had he in any way hinted at his wishes on that score. Nevertheless, he had taken private measures of his own in the whole matter. Until Cabaco's discovery was made public, the sailors had little foreseen it. To be sure, once they had been a little while out of port and all hands had finished the customary business of fitting out the whaleboats for service, Ahab was, some time after this, now and then found busying himself with making thole-pins (the pegs that hold the oars in place) with his own hands for what was thought to be one of the spare boats, and even carefully cutting the small wooden skewers that are pinned over the groove in the bow when the line is running out; when all this was noticed in him, and particularly his concern to have an extra layer of sheathing in the bottom of the boat, as if to make it better withstand the pointed pressure of his ivory limb; and also the anxiety he showed in shaping exactly the thigh-board, or clumsy cleat, as it is sometimes called — the horizontal piece in the boat's bow for bracing the knee against when darting or stabbing at the whale; when it was noticed how often he stood up in that boat with his single knee fixed in the semicircular hollow in the cleat, and with the carpenter's chisel gouged out a little here and straightened it a little there — all these things, I say, had stirred much interest and curiosity at the time. But almost everybody supposed that this particular care in preparation on Ahab's part could only be with a view to the final chase of Moby Dick, for he had already revealed his intention to hunt that mortal monster in person. But such a supposition by no means involved the faintest suspicion that any boat's crew would be assigned to that boat.

As for the lesser phantoms, whatever wonder was left about them soon faded, because on a whaler wonders never last long. Besides, every so often such unaccountable odds and ends of strange nations turn up from the unknown corners and ash-heaps of the earth to crew these floating outlaws, the whalers; and the ships themselves so often pick up such odd castaways, found drifting on the open sea on planks, scraps of wreckage, oars, whaleboats, canoes, Japanese junks blown off course, and who knows what else, that Beelzebub himself could climb up the side and go down into the cabin for a chat with the captain without stirring up any uncontrollable excitement in the forecastle.

But be all this as it may, it is certain that while the subordinate phantoms soon found their place among the crew — though still, as it were, somehow distinct from them — that hair-turbaned Fedallah remained a muffled mystery to the last. Where he came from, in a well-mannered world like this; by what unaccountable sort of tie he soon showed himself to be linked with Ahab's peculiar fortunes — indeed, so far as to have some sort of half-hinted influence; Heaven knows, it might even have been authority over him — all this nobody knew. But no one can keep up an air of indifference about Fedallah. He was such a creature as civilized, domestic people in the temperate zone see only in their dreams, and even then only dimly; but the like of him now and then glide among the unchanging Asiatic communities, especially the Oriental islands to the east of the continent — those isolated, immemorial, unalterable countries which even in these modern days still keep much of the ghostly aboriginal quality of earth's first generations, when the memory of the first man was a distinct recollection, and all men, his descendants, not knowing where he came from, eyed each other as real phantoms, and asked the sun and the moon why they were created and to what end; when, though according to Genesis the angels indeed consorted with the daughters of men, the devils also, add the uncanonical rabbis, indulged in earthly love affairs.
